FOUREX

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Two South African inventors in London win big

Summary:
Jeff Paterson and Oliver du Toit, two SA-born entrepreneurs based in Kent, UK, won Virgin Media’s "Pitch to Rich" competition. They presented their winning idea to Richard Branson for possible investment. Their idea, already in motion, is called Fourex, and comprises foreign exchange kiosks that exchange spare coins and notes for cash. Fourex allows its UK customers to deposit unsorted coins and notes in various denominations and receive pounds, euros or US dollars in return. Unusually, Fourex accepts now-defunct currencies such as German deutsche marks, Spanish pesetas and Austrian schillings. In their research ahead of setting the business up, Paterson and du Toit found that at least £3bn in unused currency is floating around the UK.

Further information:
Self-service currency exchange kiosk firm Fourex strikes gold as seed funding target exceeded.
The entrepreneurs behind a new self-service currency-exchange kiosk that allows customers to convert unwanted foreign currency into sterling, euros or US dollars, have raised nearly £100,000 more than their £275,000 target in seed funding – in just eight days. Co-founders Jeff Paterson and Oliver Du Toit have spent two years developing Fourex, a note and coin exchange machine that uses image-recognition technology to identify 150 currencies. It has been estimated by Zopa, a peer-to-peer lending company, that there is about £3billion of unused foreign currency in UK homes.The company has just signed a contract with Transport for London which will see machines being installed in Canary Wharf, King’s Cross and Blackfriars underground stations.
There will also be machines in Westfield shopping centres in London. The first machines, which can accept 300 coins a minute, will be in operation from June. The machines will also be able to accept pre-euro notes and coins such as Deutschmarks and pesetas.The founders, who have invested about £1million in the company, hope that eventually there will be about 500 machines in London, which will be emptied each day, operate in ten languages and will display the latest exchange rate. Mixed coins and notes are simply dumped into the kiosk, and the machine uses its high speed technology to identify, evaluate and exchange each and every coin or note. The kiosks accept coins and notes from over 150 currencies, as well as money from the old European currencies. (Deutschmarks, Pesetas, Schillings, etc). Local UK coins can also be converted into cash. You can choose to exchange your money directly into either pounds, euros or dollars. Yes, you can choose to be paid out in either Pounds, Euros or Dollars. Your foreign currency can be exchanged directly into either Euros or Dollars without first being converted to Pounds. This saves you being charged twice if you would like to use your leftover money as holiday money.

-------------------------------

Sir Richard Branson crowns Fourex, based in Medway City Estate, Strood, winners of Pitch to Rich competition for foreign coins exchange machine
29 June 2015by Chris Pricecprice@thekmgroup.co.uk

A company which turns unwanted foreign coins into sterling has won the support of Sir Richard Branson after winning a competition to pitch to the Virgin founder.

Fourex, founded by entrepreneurs Jeff Paterson and Oliver Du Toit, beat off competition from more than 2,500 businesses on its way to winning Pitch to Rich in London on Friday.

Its founders have developed a machine which converts unsorted coins and notes from more than 150 currencies into pounds, euros or US dollars.

Fourex units will be installed in busy London Underground stations
The kiosks will be installed at Canary Wharf, Kings Cross and Blackfriars tube stations in next month, as well as Westfield shopping centre in Stratford.

The company, based in Medway City Estate, Strood, has won a share of £1 million of prizes including advertising campaigns, a £50,000 investments and mentoring from Sir Richard Branson and his team.

Co-founder Mr Paterson said: “We’re absolutely over the moon to have won Virgin Media Businesses’ Pitch to Rich.

“It’s such an amazing achievement and we’re humbled by all of the support we have received so far.

"We’re looking forward to seeing what the rest of 2015 brings and to start rolling out the machines later this year.”

Fourex, which won the New Things category, was among nine finalists.

Sir Richard Branson said: “All nine can go on and do really well with their businesses. In the end we decided we would go with who we think will be the most likely to be the most successful in their business.”

Read the full interview with Fourex's founders inside this week’s Kent Business, free inside most paid-for KM Group newspapers.

Script:


V/O:
There are millions of people around the world who have travelled internationally, and after a trip, along with the fridge magnets, they also end up with this – left over small change.
LINK:
Money exchanges and banks refuse to exchange foreign coins or small denomination notes and if you do not spend every last penny before you return, you soon end up with a jar like this.
V/O:
Until very recently there was no way get rid of this foreign change.

But now there is, thanks to these two South African entrepreneurs we met in London. They are Oliver du Toit and Jeff Paterson. A few years ago, while both were living in Abu Dhabi, Jeff one day realised that he had accumulated a huge number of foreign coins.
Jeff:
We were working for an airline so to get a cheap ticket to India or Tailand was fairly easy. Slowly and surely over the few years I was there, developed this huge jar of money that everybody seems to have.
Oliver:
So Jeff said to me one day “I’ve got all these coins. What do I do with it?” I said: “There’s no market for it. You know it’s a waste of time.
V/O:
But Oliver nevertheless investigated the issue on-line.
LINK:
He discovered that all over the world there were literally billions and billions of rands in foreign coins their owners cannot get rid of.
Jeff:
Our research show that there’s over three billion pounds in the UK of just people with jars of low-value money and it is the same throughout the world.
V/O:
That is a cool 60 billion rand in the UK alone. With such numbers Jeff and Oliver knew that if they could find a way to help travellers cash in their spare change, they would be on to something massive.

In their spare time they set about developing technology that could recognize all foreign coins and notes and calculate its value.
Jeff:
There’s more than a hundred thousand different coins in world circulation that have a value. So we would have to be able to identify every single one of those to be able to have a business. So we had to re-invent the wheel completely.
V/O:
With a lot of hard work they eventually created recognition technology that is 99,8% accurate and it can scan a coin or note in 20 milliseconds.

To build a data base they travelled all over the world to collect as many coins and notes as possible.
LINK:
Oliver estimates that they had scanned in in excess of 3.4 million coins – from new to very worn -- to develop a comprehensive database.
V/O:
Their idea was to link the database to a machine that could automatically exchange all foreign coins and notes. But to make this a success, they would need thousands of users. They decided their first machines should be placed where there were many people. For them there was only one place – the London underground.
Oliver:
London brings over a billion people through the underground. That’s why we got to be here. We got to be where the action is.
V/O:
They relocated to London, but by then they had run out of money. They successfully crowdfunded and used the money to build working prototypes of their machine.
LINK:
Then in 2015 they heard about a novel business competition funded by Richard Branson called “Pitch to Rich”.
V/O:
It is a competition for entrepreneurs to pitch business ideas to Richard Branson and five other judges. Jeff and Oliver’s idea made it to the finals.
Jeff:
And we had two minutes to pitch. What was nice is that they picked our idea on the idea that it had the most potential to go globally and that’s why we think we won.
V/O:
The prize money was in excess of R1 mil, but more importantly, the Virgin Group also provides massive exposure, such as branding on their trains with the logo of the winners.

To see what exactly it was all about we visited Jeff and Oliver at their factory in Kent and found them tinkering with the latest version of their money changing kiosk. Their machine is a world first.
UPSOUND OLIVER:
So today we are going to present multiple currencies in coins and obviously in notes.
• On the sides of the Kiosk current exchange rates are displayed and updated by the minute.

UPSOUND:
Selecting our pay-out currencies, so we try Euros.

• On the front it has a touch screen where one can choose a currency for the pay-out
• And then you just follow simple instructions on screen

UPSOUND:
All your coins, mixed, and simultanously your notes.

• The machine scans each coin and note in a few milliseconds and determines its origin and value. It then calculates the total in a currency of your choice.
• Once the processing has been done, the machine issues receipts documenting the transaction.
• Then the machine pays out the amount exchanged in coins or notes.
Jeff:
So we make our money on the difference between what we buy the currency for and what we sell the currency just like everybody else does. However, we do not charge any extra fees or commissions.
V/O:
The 21st of October was a red letter day for Jeff and Oliver. At busy Houston Station in Central London, their first kiosk was put into operation.

The dream that started with a handful of coins in Abu Dhabi had finally become a reality, and they are about to deploy their machines worldwide. But for them, the true reward for their hard work is ultimately not financial.
Oliver:
It is not the money. It’s the excitement, it’s the journey. It’s actually developing something that is a world first. It appeals to everyone because everyone has got a cookie jar somewhere. Everyone’s got the problem, and we solved that problem.
